title: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks
description: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on hu
body: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on human rights to that of authoritarian states.The diplomatic row was initially sparked last week, when the US joined North Korea and Russia in voting against extending Volker Turk's term as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. After the vote on Friday, France's UN mission criticised the US and compared it to North Korea and Russia. "The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore," it posted on X, external.In response, US ambassador Mike Waltz accused France of voting for a human rights chief who had been "lecturing" democratic countries while "cozying up to the world's worst oppressors", without elaborating on what he meant.Turk has criticised Russia's war in Ukraine and Israel's military conduct in Gaza.The US team's walkout came while France's ambassador Jerome Bonnafont was speaking during an emergency Security Council meeting on Russia's war in Ukraine.US ambassador Dan Negrea said the delegation would continue to make similar protests until France "renounces their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric".The fight over Turk's second term, which was passed with 144 states in favour, 10 against and 13 abstentions, reflects tensions between Washington and the United Nations.The Trump administration has cut funding for UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of its entities.On Friday, US ambassador Jeff Bartos criticised Turk's reappointment and said "there will be consequences" to the assembly which "tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts". "The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding," he said.However, French ambassador Bonnafont described Turk as "a voice of conscience" who demonstrated "rigor and impartiality" during his first term.Deputy UN spokesperson Farhan Haq declined to comment on the US walkout, adding the UN expected all member states to respect the decision.

schema.headline: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks

title: Shots fired at US consulate in Toronto for a second time this year
description: Toronto police said they were investigating the latest attack with the help of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and international law enforcem
body: Toronto police said they were investigating the latest attack with the help of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and international law enforcement partners.Supt Jonathan Ko with the RCMP called it "another troubling incident", while the city's mayor, Olivia Chow, called the attack "brazen". "I want to say to the person or persons responsible: We will get you," Chow added.The shooting occurred around 04:45 local time (09:45 BST). Officers said they recovered one shell casing at the scene and damage to the building's facade. At least two individuals were inside the consulate at the time, Toronto Police Deputy Chief Frank Barredo said, but he noted the building is "very heavily fortified" and those inside likely did not hear the gun shot.He added that the investigation remains ongoing and that police across the city have been asked to lookout for the potential suspects."We will bring the people responsible to justice," Barredo said.In a post on X, the US consulate in Toronto thanked the police for their response. Police have been stationed outside the consulate since March, when shots were fired outside the building in what police at the time called a "national security incident". No one was injured in that attack. In June, police carried out raids in relation to the shooting. Police officer Marc Pinizzotto, 43, was killed during the operation. Police later arrested several suspects aged 18 and 19 for allegedly carrying out a string of shootings, including the March attack outside the consulate, as part of a larger gun-for-hire network.Two Jewish-owned bakeries in the city were also targeted, at least one by gunfire, over the weekend. Police said on Monday there was currently nothing to link the two incidents, but they did not rule out a connection. "I'm totally disgusted by the shootings and vandalism that took place in Toronto over the last few days," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said.Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said he was "appalled" and added: "Law enforcement has my full support as they conduct a thorough investigation and hold those responsible to account."In May, US officials arrested an Iraqi national, 32-year-old Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, for allegedly planning more than a dozen attacks in North America and Europe targeting Jewish institutions and US interests, including the one at the US consulate in Toronto.Police in Toronto have not said if al-Saadi is linked to their investigation, and they have not specified a motive for this latest consulate shooting.

schema.headline: Shots fired at US consulate in Toronto for a second time this year

title: Ariana Grande sues hackers who leaked music and videos
description: Pop star Ariana Grande has filed a lawsuit against two unidentified hackers who, she claims, leaked unreleased music and studio footage after gaining
body: Pop star Ariana Grande has filed a lawsuit against two unidentified hackers who, she claims, leaked unreleased music and studio footage after gaining access to her collaborators' computers.In papers filed in Los Angeles and reported by US media outlets, the singer alleged the hackers had targeted photographers and producers' in order to access material that was sold "on the dark web" for "significant sums of money"."In 2023 alone, 45 unreleased songs belonging to Ms Grande were hacked, stolen, and leaked," the documents said. "Since her music debut in 2011, hundreds of similar leaks have taken place."Her lawyers said she was initiating legal action to uncover the identity of the hackers.Grande has previously expressed her desire to hold hackers accountable for leaking unreleased music.During an interview with the Zach Sang show in 2024, she spoke about a song called Fantasize, written with Swedish pop savant Max Martin, which went viral after being posted online."Before I left for Wicked - [there were] a few studio sessions that I did which are all over TikTok, thank you so much, I'll see you in jail. Literally," she said."Those were all written for a TV show, for something that was not for me, so Fantasize comes out, crazy, was stolen... These pirates, crooks, illegal!"Her legal case outlined an alleged pattern of illegal behaviour, in which the accounts of Grande's co-workers were systematically targeted over several years.In 2025, it claimed, the defendants hacked into the mobile device of a producer who had collaborated with Grande and accessed unreleased masters, demos and footage from recording sessions.The previous year, the suit claimed, hackers created an email account impersonating a photographer, and persuaded a digital technician to send them unreleased photos that belonged to Grande.The singer accused the hackers of violating the "sacred relationship that exists between her and her fans" and is suing for invasion of privacy, violation of California computer hacking laws, and conversion. Her lawyers said the "malicious invasion of Ms. Grande's privacy and disruption of her career have caused her substantial and irreparable harm due to this breach of privacy."The court filing comes as Grande prepares for the release of her eighth studio album, Petal, this Friday.She is currently in the middle of a world tour, which is due to hit the UK in August.Grande previously hinted the concerts would be her last for "a long time"."I'm going to give it my all and it's going to be beautiful," she told Amy Poehler's Good Hang podcast, external. "I think that's why I'm doing it because I'm like: 'One last hurrah' - for now."

schema.headline: Ariana Grande sues hackers who leaked music and videos

title: 'Do the right thing': Savannah Guthrie pleads to mother's kidnappers
description: It was one of two ransom notes believed to be credible that were addressed to Nancy Guthrie's family and sent to news media shortly after her January
body: It was one of two ransom notes believed to be credible that were addressed to Nancy Guthrie's family and sent to news media shortly after her January kidnapping. The first demanded millions in Bitcoin for her release; the second stated that she had died, according to US media, which cited unnamed sources. Why the trail went cold in Nancy Guthrie caseIn her latest video posted on Monday, Savannah Guthrie addressed the possible kidnappers. "It has been months since our mum was taken from us," Guthrie said. "Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part, and we will never stop looking for her. We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts."She added: "Help us bring this situation to an end. For all of us, no matter where we've been and what we've done, I believe there is always a way home. Please make the right choice."The Pima County Sheriff's Department has not commented on the contents of any apparent ransom notes, but the department said their investigation "remains active and ongoing".The BBC's US partner, CBS News, and other news outlets reported that law enforcement had requested that media hold off publishing details of any of the notes while they investigated Nancy Guthrie's disappearance.The FBI and Pima County have spent months investigating her mysterious abduction from her Arizona home. Nancy Guthrie, who needs daily medication, vanished sometime after she was dropped off at her home by relatives on the January evening almost six months ago. She failed to show up the following morning at a friend's house to watch a virtual Sunday church service.Earlier this year, authorities released images of a masked and armed suspect who covered the  front door camera at Nancy Guthrie's home before her disappearance. An initial ransom note was sent the day after she went missing and demanded millions in Bitcoin for her release.It gave specific details about her home, as well as details about her bedroom and the home's surroundings, investigators told CBS.Savannah Guthrie has said some ransom notes sent to the family were believed to be fake. She has said that her mother may no longer be alive.

schema.headline: 'Do the right thing': Savannah Guthrie pleads to mother's kidnappers

title: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez
description: Figure caption, BBC reports from outside court after judge rules singer D4vd will stand trial for murderBySareen HabeshianShaimaa Khalil and Sam Mulic
body: Figure caption, BBC reports from outside court after judge rules singer D4vd will stand trial for murderBySareen HabeshianShaimaa Khalil and Sam MulickReporting fromcourthouse in Los AngelesUpdated 8 hours agoA judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of a teenage girl.The decision came after a five-day preliminary hearing, in which Los Angeles prosecutors questioned a dozen witnesses and displayed graphic photographic evidence as 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez's family watched on.The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, is accused of killing the girl, whose remains were found last September in a Tesla registered to his address.Burke, 21, has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing her.Burke is scheduled to be charged on 31 August. The trial is to start within 90 days of that date.Prosecutors have alleged Burke stabbed the teen before dismembering her body after years of sexual abuse.They allege he killed her because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.Evidence read in court on Monday showed threats Hernandez made to Burke on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl."I swear to GOD I will kill u", one expletive-laden text said, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on.The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.During questioning at the hearing on Monday, Detective Corey Farrell of the Los Angeles Police Department said text messages indicated that the defendant and the girl had attended church with her family.  In response to the defence, the detective said he was aware the teen had misrepresented her age to the defendant, telling him she was 16 and 18 at different times.Burke's defence lawyers argued there was not sufficient evidence that he had committed the crime.They said her parents were aware of what was going on between them and had even given written consent for her to travel to London with Burke for a week. The defence highlighted texts on the 22nd and the 23rd of April that suggested Celeste had insisted on going to Burke's Hollywood Hills home and that he had argued against her coming before agreeing to send her an Uber on the night of the 23rd.He "repeatedly expressed love and care for Ms Hernandez after they broke up", defence attorney Marilyn Bednarski said in court.The medical examiner's inability to prove how the two penetrating wounds found in the girl occurred and the lack of surveillance video capturing Burke being home on the night of 23 April showed a lack of evidence, the defence argued.Image source, Getty ImagesLos Angeles County Superior Court Judge Charlaine Olmedo ruled that evidence presented during the preliminary hearing provided probable cause for a trial.Burke is charged with murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14, and unlawful mutilation of human remains."The people have met their burden on all counts," Judge Olmedo said.She found that prosecutors met the threshold for the charge of murder with special circumstances, including lying in wait, motive for financial gain and eliminating a witness.Following the hearing, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said his office only presented a fraction of the evidence it had against Burke, and that it would present everything in the coming trial.Hochman also said his office had not yet determined if it would pursue the death penalty against Burke.Listen to the BBC's Fame Under Fire podcast which brings you the latest from inside the Los Angeles courtroom at the D4vd preliminary hearing.Gruesome images of the girl's dismembered corpse were shown in court during the preliminary hearing.A homicide detective testified that Burke had ordered a body bag, chainsaws, an inflatable pool and a shovel online in the days after Celeste's death.Prosecutors highlighted records that revealed Burke ordered chainsaws and a shovel to his residence after April 23. They allege he used a chainsaw to dismember Hernadez's body.However, Los Angeles Police Department criminalist Lauren Wallace testified that the chainsaws found in his garage tested negative for the presence of blood and were not tested for DNA thereafter, a point the defence highlighted in their attempt to prove the evidence presented was inconclusive.However, investigators were unable to locate a third, 10-inch Makita chainsaw, which prosecutors claim Burke also ordered following Hernandez's death.

schema.headline: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez

title: Trump says Iran war talks taking place during lull in strikes
description: US President Donald Trump has said "there are very friendly negotiations going on" about the conflict with Iran, after the warring sides did not excha
body: US President Donald Trump has said "there are very friendly negotiations going on" about the conflict with Iran, after the warring sides did not exchange strikes for a third straight day.He expressed optimism for an end to the war on Monday, telling reporters aboard Air Force One: "I think there's a good chance that something could happen."However, he warned that Washington would "go back to doing what we were doing" before the pause in fighting if the latest negotiations failed.Tehran has denied that any direct negotiations are taking place.Trump said he had decided to pause US strikes on Iran on Friday because the countries mediating between them had asked him to give the talks another chance. Iran has also halted its attacks.The pause follows nearly two weeks of daily US strikes and tit-for-tat attacks, effectively unravelling the ceasefire struck in June.The US military said at the time that its strikes were aimed to "degrade Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz" - a global route for transporting oil.The price of oil on Monday fell by more than 9% to $87.59 a barrel at one point on hopes the conflict could be de-escalated.Aboard the presidential plane, Trump also dismissed media reports that after five months of fighting, US ammunition stockpiles were now running low."We have a lot of ammunition. We have a lot of the mid-level stuff too, more than we could ever use, no matter what," Trump said. "But we have a lot. I'd like to have more."He said a "lot of equipment" was being built, in particular Patriots - highly valued US-made anti-ballistic missiles."That system is going up. We have a lot," he said.Meanwhile, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said the US military "has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of President Trump's strategic goals and beyond, and Operation Epic Fury has exposed what happens when you mess with the United States.""Even still, the president has urged our defence contractors to constantly produce more made-in-America weapons, which are the best in the world," the spokesperson added.

schema.headline: Trump says Iran war talks taking place during lull in strikes

title: Ukraine dismisses Iranian threats as Caspian Sea strike directly links wars
description: Ukraine has dismissed Iranian threats of retaliation, following Kyiv's targeting of an Iranian cargo vessel in the Caspian Sea on Saturday.The inciden
body: Ukraine has dismissed Iranian threats of retaliation, following Kyiv's targeting of an Iranian cargo vessel in the Caspian Sea on Saturday.The incident marked the first direct link between the wars in Iran and Ukraine."Iran's threats are unjustified and groundless," Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on X this afternoon."The regime in Tehran is a direct accomplice to Russian aggression against Ukraine, fuelling Moscow's criminal war with weapons that have killed Ukrainians since 2022," he wrote, referring to the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.President Volodymyr Zelensky on Saturday announced that Ukrainian forces had achieved "very good results" in long-range strikes in the Caspian Sea, including against vessels used to transport military cargo linked to Iran.The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said its drones had hit an oil platform in the northern Caspian Sea, along with a Russian missile boat and "cargo ships that are under international sanctions."Iran's ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, told Iran's state news agency that the "Anna" ship had been anchored about 5km (3 miles) from the mouth of the Volga River when it was targeted. Ukraine's ambassador to Israel, Yevgen Korniychuk, said the vessel had been carrying components for drones and missiles from Iran to Russia, not civilian cargo.Speaking to Israel's N12, he insisted that Ukraine and Israel were confronting the same "axis of evil" on different fronts. Iran reacted with fury to the assault which it said had killed one sailor and injured several others. The foreign ministry said Iran had "never intervened in the conflict between Russia and Ukraine."Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the attack represented "a blatant UN Charter violation done at Israel's behest to drag Europe into its war."The incident "CANNOT GO UNANSWERED," he wrote on X.In his own statement on Monday, Sybiha included Araghchi's post, with the words "Iranian lies" posted across it.He also accused Iran of trying to shift attention away from Russia's attacks on ships carrying grain from Ukrainian ports, which he said were threatening global food security.For its part, Ukraine has been relentlessly targeting Russian shadow fleet of oil tankers, looking to choke off a major source of revenue for the Kremlin.Along with drone strikes on oil depots and the Wildberries online retail warehouses, what Zelensky calls Ukraine's "long-range sanctions campaign" is having increasingly serious impact on the Russian economy.But some experts question the wisdom of Kyiv's decision to pick a fight with Iran."The main idea... is to disrupt trading routes and cause as much damage as possible," former intelligence official Ivan Stupak told the BBC. "But it's not a good idea for Ukraine to have another battlefront with Iran. It's not good for us," he added.Olha Polishchuk from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled) said the Caspian Sea strike was "less about opening a new front against Tehran" and instead could be seen as an extension of Kyiv's targeting of networks supporting the Russian war effort."Targeting that route allows Kyiv to put further pressure on Russia's supply networks beyond the traditional battlefield," she said.

schema.headline: Ukraine dismisses Iranian threats as Caspian Sea strike directly links wars

title: Number of suspects in fatal Bite of Seattle food festival shooting rises to three
description: Seattle police say they now believe at least three people were involved in a fatal shooting at a food festival on Sunday.Police initially said two sus
body: Seattle police say they now believe at least three people were involved in a fatal shooting at a food festival on Sunday.Police initially said two suspects were thought to have been shooting at each other at the annual Bite of Seattle food festival at the Space Needle - one of the city's most popular tourist spots.However, court papers relating to the arrest of one of these, a 15-year-old, on Monday revealed they now think there is a third attacker. One is still being sought by police, while the other is thought to have been killed at the scene. Three people were killed in the shooting and at least four others were injured, including a two-year old boy. The teenage suspect waived his initial appearance in court on Monday, and he was remanded in custody pending trial, according to local media.Ahead of the hearing, police revealed in court documents that they believe that three suspects may have fired shots during the "gunfight".Court papers filed by the police say investigators are searching for "at least one other unknown suspect", according to local media. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, speaking at a news conference on Monday, said: "Police continue to look for a third possible suspect."The three people who died on Sunday were 19-year-old Junior Cee Niko Semo, Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56, according to the King County medical examiner. Police now believe that Semo was involved in the gunfight.Two deaths were confirmed at the scene, and one person died in hospital.Two guns were recovered at the scene, police said. Speaking on Monday afternoon, Assistant Police Chief Nicole Powell said that preliminary information indicated the shooting may have been "gang-related".She added that the 15-year-old suspect and the 19-year-old who was killed are believed to be "associated with each other". She declined to describe their connection.Sunday was the final day of the annual three-day free food festival, which draws some 350,000 people each year.Videos shared online showed people crouched on the ground, taking cover behind pillars and shelves of merchandise in the Space Needle's lobby during the shooting.Leanne Coles, another witness, told CBS News, the BBC's US partner: "Everybody started running, and so we just ran too, and we ran through the garden and we ducked and we decided to keep running with the crowd."Faith Adia Hunter told the Associated Press news agency that one of the shooters was near her and her friends when they heard the shots, sending them fleeing for shelter in the Seattle Children's Museum."We were right next to him when it started so we took off running," she said. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said on social media: "My prayers are with the families of the victims, and the responders as they work to keep people safe." Mayor Wilson also condemned the shooting as an "act of horrific violence".

schema.headline: Number of suspects in fatal Bite of Seattle food festival shooting rises to three

title: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'
description: "The release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate," Wilson noted. "This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas... translations of Odyssey
body: "The release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate," Wilson noted. "This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas... translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves... [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments."Nolan... is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful."But she was left largely disappointed by the three-hour epic"I had hoped that Nolan's affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters," she wrote."But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality... the film's vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants."Wilson added that her teenagers had "had a good time" seeing the blockbuster at the cinema."It's a family-friendly audiovisual spectacle, like an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display - and with about the same level of narrative and emotional depth," she said."There are more female characters than in most Nolan movies, thanks to the source material. But none of them has much to say, in contrast to the characterisations in the poem."During his press tour for the film, Sir Christopher told Empire magazine, external that he used the opening line of Wilson's translation ("Tell me about a complicated man") as a guide for his Odysseus, played by Matt Damon.In contrast to Wilson's take, the latest adaptation has received rapturous reviews from film critics.It is the director's first movie since 2023's Oppenheimer, which won the Academy Award for best picture.The Telegraph declared The Odyssey the "film of the year", while Metro added that the movie would "change cinema forever".The Times described it as "a masterpiece in every way", and the Standard praised the film as a "colossal piece of cinema".The Odyssey, which was released earlier this month, stars Matt Damon, Zendaya, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, Anne Hathaway, Charlize Theron and Lupita Nyong'o.It follows Odysseus (Damon), the Greek king of Ithaca, on his long and perilous journey home from the Trojan War to rescue his wife and son (Hathaway and Holland).

schema.headline: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'

title: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress
description: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with t
body: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with the sun disappearing behind", with an "orange-like filter" over the city.Though De Abreu said he is less concerned about his flat which lies on the other side of the river, he "can see a number of people worried about what is to come".Elsewhere, Rachel Hanberry told BBC Radio 5 Live that her beachfront home in Biscarrosse Plage, which lies about 63km (40 miles) from Bordeaux, is located next to the town's evacuation point. "Everyone came here on Thursday night," she said. "People had nowhere to go. We offered our home to people."The community there has "lost so much", she added. "The stress and trauma that you feel as someone living here is immense." About 700km away, in Cotignac in the south-east of France, Jo Barnes and her family returned to their home on Saturday, having evacuated for four days after a fire rapidly moved towards their property. "A wall of orange flames came roaring up over the hill," Barnes said. "On Friday afternoon, the fire came back to our area... within 10 metres of the back of our house, we have a gas tank here, it was all very dramatic." Though the surrounding hillside was blackened and charred, the town of Cotignac was undamaged and the Barnes' family home left intact. In the central Madrid region of Spain, where more than 27,000 hectares (66,000 acres) have burnt, residents have faced similar ordeals. "Everyone had to get out of the village quickly, it was a critical situation and people were scared," Olga Congacha told AFP news agency.She and her husband did not take much: "[We] left with all that we could grab, our important documents, some clothes".In the eastern Castellón province, Ricardo Pozo told AFP that he had "never seen a fire this intense before". "I've seen major fires, but on television. Nothing like this, here and now." Maria Garcia, who lives in Betxí - also in the Castellón province - described to Reuters how the fires had put life on pause for those who evacuated: "You can't go out to work, you can't go about your daily life." "You can see the mountains you've known your whole life burning," she added.The wildfires have also upended plans for holidaymakers. James Hillier had been visiting his son in the seaside community of Lacanau about 42 km (26 miles) east of Bordeaux in the Gironde department."The whole town got consumed by smoke," he told the BBC. "There was ash falling from the sky and I noticed a big lump of it landed on my hand."He and his wife left the town for Bordeaux on Saturday, but found that in the city "the air was acrid - it stung your eyes and people were wearing masks". They have since left to go to somewhere in the north of the France instead. Sarah from Hertfordshire realised that her family would have to cut their week-long holiday in Bordeaux short because of the smoke. "We sealed all the apartment up, but it still had a really strong smell of smoke everywhere. It was quite worrying," she said.She then warned her sister-in-law Georgia, whose family had been due to join them in the Bordeaux region in Lacanau, not to come. Georgia booked to stay in another region instead.Georgia said she has not been able to secure a refund from her accommodation operator because the fire had not yet reached Lacanau at the time of cancellation. "If we don't find a solution with them we currently stand to lose over £3,500," Georgia added.

schema.headline: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress

title: Zinedine Zidane: Former Real Madrid manager appointed as France head coach
description: Former Real Madrid manager Zinedine Zidane has been confirmed as the head coach of the France national team.Didier Deschamps, France's longest-serving
body: Former Real Madrid manager Zinedine Zidane has been confirmed as the head coach of the France national team.Didier Deschamps, France's longest-serving manager, ended his 14-year stint in charge after the nation's semi-final exit to Spain at the 2026 World Cup. Zidane, a World Cup winner with France in 1998, has been out of management since leaving Real Madrid for a second time as head coach in 2021. The 54-year-old, widely considered to be France's greatest player, will sign a contract that will see him lead the nation through the 2030 World Cup qualifiers. On being appointed, he said it was "a great source of pride" to lead the French national side following their fourth-place finish at the World Cup."I've often said it: there's nothing greater than the French national team. So it's a joy and obviously a great source of pride to become the manager of this French national team," he added."It's also a responsibility. I want to thank [French Football Federation] president Philippe Diallo, the executive committee, and the French Football Federation for their confidence and acknowledge the 14 years of service from Didier and his staff. "I also have a special thought today for all my coaches. Needless to say, I have high ambitions for the French national team."Diallo described the new head coach as a "legend" of French football."The appointment of Zinedine Zidane as head coach of the French national team is a source of immense pride for the French Football Federation," he said."It marks the meeting of a legend in the history of Les Bleus, who has become one of the most decorated and respected coaches of his generation, and a team with rare potential, driven by the highest ambitions."Zidane's predecessor Deschamps guided France to three major finals over his 14-year reign, helping the country to their second World Cup success with victory in 2018.Zidane's first competitive fixture in charge will be a Nations League trip to Turkey on 25 September.After retiring as a player following the 2006 World Cup, Zidane did not enter management until 2014, when he became coach of Real Madrid Castilla - the club's B team.He stepped up to become the first team manager in January 2016, and by the end of that season had led them to Champions League success with a victory over city rivals Atletico Madrid in the final on penalties.That was the first of three successive Champions League titles for Madrid, making them the first club to win back-to-back European crowns in the Champions League era, and the first to win three titles in a row since Bayern Munich in 1976.He also won La Liga in 2016-17, but departed after the following season, saying change was needed at the Bernabeu.However, Zidane returned to Madrid in March 2019 with the club in poor form, and won another Spanish league title in 2019-20.He also oversaw a period of extensive spending at Madrid, including the signings of Eden Hazard and Rodrygo.But Zidane left at the end of a trophyless 2020-21 campaign, and has not managed since.Zidane has long been courted to become France manager and was first linked with the job after the team was knocked out of the 2010 World Cup in the group stage.Some 16 years later, he has finally taken on the role and will lead the French into qualifying for Euro 2028.Zidane started his playing career at Cannes in 1989, then played for Bordeaux until joining Juventus in 1996.An attacking midfielder, he helped the Italian side win back-to-back Serie A titles and reach successive Champions League finals, before joining Real Madrid in 2001.Zidane moved for £66 million, then the world record transfer fee, as part of Real Madrid's Galacticos era alongside other global stars including Ronaldo, Luis Figo and David Beckham.He began delivering on that fee in the 2002 Champions League final, scoring a stunning volleyed winner as Madrid beat Bayer Leverkusen 2-1 at Hampden Park.For the France national team, Zidane made his greatest contribution as a player with two headed goals in the 1998 World Cup final in Paris.France beat Brazil 3-0 to win the World Cup for the first time, and Zidane won the Ballon d'Or later that year.Zidane was also part of the France team that won Euro 2000, but endured disappointing campaigns in the 2002 World Cup and Euro 2004.He retired from international football in 2004, but was persuaded to return during qualifying for the 2006 World Cup.Zidane was a key player in France advancing through the knock-out stages to the final against Italy - his final match as a professional footballer - and scored the opener with a Panenka penalty off the crossbar after seven minutes.But Italy equalised and the game went to extra time, during which Zidane headbutted Marco Materazzi and was dismissed. Italy went on to win the final on penalties.

schema.headline: Zinedine Zidane: Former Real Madrid manager appointed as France head coach

title: A Japanese town wrestles with identity after protests over its first mosque
description: Today, it's a field of grass. But soon, it'll be the site of the first mosque in this Japanese town."It makes me worry about how our community might c
body: Today, it's a field of grass. But soon, it'll be the site of the first mosque in this Japanese town."It makes me worry about how our community might change," says long-time resident Noriko Izumizawa.Plans to build an Islamic religious site in Fujisawa, a laid-back seaside town about an hour's drive south of Tokyo, have sparked a wide range of emotions.There is anger and fear, as well as hope and acceptance, exposing the growing anxieties over immigration and social change as Japan grapples with a labour shortage from a shrinking and ageing population.Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive, Japan is increasingly relying on foreign workers to fill open jobs. That means an influx of immigrants with various cultures, languages, religions and ways of being.So the debate that is playing out in towns like Fujisawa across the country is one that goes to the heart of how Japan sees itself.Izumizawa is not alone in the way she feels. She is among a group of Fujisawa residents who are anxious about the increasingly visible Muslim community. She says that the polarising debates around immigration in the US and Europe have also contributed to her unease.Earlier this year, anti-mosque protests flared up at the local train station, where thousands took to the streets to object to the proposed construction of the mosque. Some argue that a mosque much larger than the nearby Japanese Shinto shrine is disrespectful.There have also been reports of hate speech and misinformation spreading on Japanese social media. Local outlets say mosques have been receiving abusive phone calls and emails, some of which has prompted anti-hate groups to organise counter protests calling for no hate.Hiroki Suzuka, who manages a coffee shop opposite the road where the Fujisawa mosque is set to be built, calls for greater understanding and dialogue."I'm not particularly opposed, but I wouldn't say I'm strongly in favour either," Suzuka said."I think the first step is to learn about them, what Islam is, what kind of people they are, and what values and perspectives they hold. It begins with having an open mind and a desire to understand each other."Businessman Mohamed Mohideen has lived in Osaka for the past 39 years. He moved from his home country Sri Lanka in 1987 for better work opportunities during the economic bubble.He has dealt gemstones and later worked in trade, exporting used cars to countries like Sri Lanka and Pakistan.He moved at a time, he says, when there were far fewer foreign residents.But Mohideen feels that compared to back then, local people have become hostile and started making hurtful remarks at Muslims, both online and in person."On social media, there are countless comments like, 'Get out of Japan' and 'Go back to your own country,'" Mohideen said. "People have also started coming to the mosque and shouting abuse."Mohideen goes to the Osaka mosque every day for prayers and other duties as a member of the local Islamic community. He says he has never felt that his life was in danger.Despite having good relationships with neighbours for many years, Mohideen has noticed the shift in attitude towards Muslims more recently."Now, I feel that people are afraid of us."The verbal abuse has worsened in recent years. He recalled members of his Muslim community being called terrorists, accused of making bombs, and being told to get out of Japan."When that happens, the only thing we can do is be patient. They're trying to provoke a fight or create a confrontation. They want to see how long we'll tolerate it," Mohideen explained."So we stay calm, speak gently, and treat them kindly, because Japanese people generally don't know much about Islam."Still, he thinks there is some shared responsibility for the rift."We focused only on our work and, for a long time, didn't make enough effort to help people understand who we are. We also didn't do enough to become part of the society," he said."From now on, I want to work harder to increase dialogue and build better mutual understanding."Shakeel Mohamed, 61, has been representing the Yashio mosque in Saitama prefecture for the past decade. He had worked as a construction site supervisor for 26 years after moving to Japan from Pakistan and speaks fluent Japanese.Mohamed says the most important thing is to follow Japan's rules, including sorting refuse properly, obeying parking laws, and wearing helmets when riding your bicycle."We make every effort to respect the way things are done in Japan and to follow the rules," he said. "Courtesy is important too, even something as simple as greeting people."He said Japanese locals in Yashio refer to the area's Pakistani community as "Yashio-stan"."Of course, there are some Pakistanis who behave badly, but they're only a small minority. And the same is true of Japanese people."Japan is wrestling with its identity in the face of huge demographic shifts.Muslims in Japan, including foreign residents and Japanese believers, numbered roughly 420,000 at the end of 2024, up from 230,000 in 2019, according to Hirofumi Tanada, a professor emeritus at Waseda University who studies the faith in Japan.The country's growing Muslim population also reflects a greater nationwide trend. The foreign resident population – which mainly comes from China, Vietnam, South Korea and the Philippines - surpassed four million in 2025. A record 2.57 million of them work in Japan, according to government data. In the same year, Japan's population declined by nearly 1 million.Government officials have long avoided describing the country as an immigration country, but push visas that are seen as more temporary than permanent. Critics describe this as a "stealth" immigration system.But even then, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has adopted a highly conservative stance against large-scale immigration. In June 2026, the Japanese government decided to raise visa fees for foreign nationals fivefold, after not having increased the amount for nearly 50 years.Now, the government is planning to increase the number of employees at the Immigration Services Agency by about 230 people, aiming to strengthen enforcement against foreigners illegally overstaying. Officials may also introduce a limit to manage the number of foreign residents in the country.As immigrant communities become more visible, the country is being forced to confront a question it has long tried to avoid: Can Japan become a more diverse country while preserving its sense of identity and cohesion that it values?Back in Fujisawa, Izumizawa admits she has never had a negative experience with a Muslim neighbour herself."The truth is, maybe I just fear the unknown," she shrugs.Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi

schema.headline: A Japanese town wrestles with identity after protests over its first mosque

title: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
description: As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an a
body: As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an additional challenge to deal with: dangerously misleading videos created with Artificial Intelligence (AI).Powerful storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media platforms –  these include images of dead bodies floating in floodwaters, the false depiction of severe flooding in areas actually not affected and others with blatantly fake details of emergency response efforts.In some areas, videos containing false information about power outages prompted residents to panic buy emergency supplies.Other videos capitalise on real-life incidents. Flooding in Hengzhou city, Guangxi in early July caused hundreds of snakes to escape from a breeding farm. Then fake images were also published showing crocodiles being released into a river.In an already tense and dangerous situation involving mass evacuations and complex rescue operations, authorities want to avoid panic. Now they fear that AI technology - which China is pouring billions of dollars into - is providing simple, accessible tools that can be used to trick the public."Many of these content creators use disaster news to try to gain followers, knowing that more sensational or exaggerated content will garner more likes and more views. They are deliberately fabricating information to grab people's attention," Huang Zhihua, Deputy Chief in charge of online public security for Zhejiang Police Department told Chinese state media.In recent weeks, there have been arrests and punishment – ranging from detention awaiting criminal prosecution to fines – for the creation of bogus reports and video content.But experts are warning that an unprecedented crisis of misinformation could be looming.In an article published by the newspaper of the Communist Party's Central Party School, Professor Chen Bin said, "AI dramatically lowers the technical barriers to producing false information. Individuals no longer require sophisticated technical skills. By simply prompting AI tools, they can rapidly generate convincing text, images, audio and video… which is highly realistic but entirely fabricated content, manufactured on a large scale."Professor Gao Fuping, from the East China University of Political Science and Law, told the BBC that motivation for the publishing of such false content ranges from those who do it "to create something amusing without thinking about the consequences", to those who want to "generate traffic for personal gain" or those who wish to deliberately "cause panic or social unrest"."Some users think the online world is anonymous and unregulated or that they cannot be traced," he said.There have been calls for all AI-generated content to be clearly stamped but other users can then just re-edit the material removing the markings.Professor Xu Xiaoke from Beijing Normal University told the BBC that greater efforts were also needed to verify geographic locations with timestamps and the checking of image sources."That said, I would also stress that detection technology still lags behind generation technology. We're in a constant cat-and-mouse game. So we should not assume that technology alone can identify AI-generated content with the click of a button," he warned.The Chinese government is embracing AI in its bid to become the leading tech superpower.In 2017,  it announced that AI would be "the main driving force" of the country's progress.Vast sums of money is pouring into AI businesses seeking more capital, fuelling domestic competition. The state-controlled wire service Xinhua reports that the country has over 6,000 "AI companies".In this climate,  Prof Xu believes that China needs to build "trusted information infrastructure". This could include official government early warning systems and disaster interfaces which news organisations can access.But there have been instances of official sources, including government-controlled media, deliberately downplaying disasters, which has led to some public mistrust in this area.Earlier in July, local journalists were asked to "soften" their language to describe a major breach in the wall of the Liulan Dam near Naning as an "opening" or "gap".Officials appeared to be trying to make the breach sound less alarming but the consequences were deadly.  Water bursting through the broken dam led to at least 26 deaths downstream.And this is not an isolated incident.In 2021, local officials were arrested, accused of concealing or underreporting 139 deaths in Henan province.Incidents like these have resulted in a trust vacuum that has made it much easier for bad actors to spread fake content.But police are imploring people to trust accredited sources during emergencies."When encountering disaster-related information from an unknown source, approach it with scepticism and rely on official announcements," Gao Kai from the Ningbo Public Security Bureau said.He also tried to reassure the public that the creators of false information would be caught, saying that "the internet is not a lawless zone. Public security authorities will continue to intensify efforts to crack down on illegal online activity"."We've created a specialised task force to monitor social media closely, especially short video platforms. They will investigate and handle these cases quickly, cracking down in a very strict manner".Punishment could range from a fine to up to seven years in prison if the fallout of the misinformation is serious enough.On 23 July, China's Cyberspace Administration also announced a nationwide crackdown on fake internet content related to floods and other disasters, ordering its local branches to focus on catching out fabricated data, malicious editing, staged scenes, misattributed historical events and those impersonating officials. In addition, it called on social media platforms to strengthen the review of the content they are publishing.Prof Gao believes "the answer is public education combined with law enforcement", saying that there was a "need to publicise real cases where people have been punished."He added that "the harm caused by AI-generated fake content is ultimately the result of how people choose to use the technology - not the technology itself", adding that existing laws were sufficient to deal with it.However, others are not so confident.  Professor Chen pointed out that "AI technology continues to evolve much faster than legal frameworks. As new legal questions emerge, AI misinformation remains a considerable challenge."Shanghai and Washington based lawyer Peter Pang says lawyers around the world are seeing an explosion in the number of cases dealing with these issues.He believes that the companies that create AI apps and the platforms used to publish fake videos and other material must be held legally accountable along with the people who create misinformation."The first line would be the platforms, because they're the ones that are the enablers. They're the ones that allow this to go out," he told the BBC.He used a hypothetical example of a person who runs over a pedestrian following panic induced by a fake post on social media."The video creator might say 'you ran over somebody. That's your problem. I didn't do it.' But let's think it through. You created the foundation from which people reacted. If you created that panic, you need to have responsibility for consequences that occur."And Professor Xu warns that "AI-generated misinformation is likely to increase not only in volume but in the speed with which it spreads.""Looking ahead, political elections, public health emergencies, armed conflicts, natural disasters and issues affecting people's livelihoods are all likely to become high-risk areas for AI-generated misinformation."Instead of waiting for false information to go viral before trying to contain it, governments and platforms should now be preparing in advance."

schema.headline: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos

title: Anger as Berlin Pride attacker revealed to have been freed weeks earlier
description: Prosecutors say that in 2025, Ballout decided to try to join Islamic State group's armed struggle in Syria, travelling via Turkey to Lebanon. In Leban
body: Prosecutors say that in 2025, Ballout decided to try to join Islamic State group's armed struggle in Syria, travelling via Turkey to Lebanon. In Lebanon, they say, he met several people he believed were members of IS.He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict.Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany, where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention.In May this year, a Berlin court sentenced Ballout to a juvenile sentence of one year and ten months, for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state".The sentence was suspended while prosecutors appealed against the verdict, calling for a longer sentence.Ballout was released and placed under the supervision of a probation officer.Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told RTL that the decision to impose a suspended sentence was "certainly incomprehensible... given the level of danger involved in this case".He said the authorities were investigating how that happened.Berlin's Governing Mayor, Kai Wegner from the centre-right Christian Democrat party (CDU), said he was dumbstruck at the way the Berlin judiciary had handled Ballout's case."He was sentenced... under juvenile criminal law," he told RBB TV. "And then, unfortunately, the court handed down a suspended sentence. I don't want to pass judgement on that – that's the independence of the judiciary – but I'm really at a loss for words."The opposition far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party described the attack as a total failure of security policy."If an Islamist threat known to the police was able to carry out such an act, a thorough investigation must be carried out to establish why he was still able to move about freely in the first place," said Martin Hess, the AfD's home affairs spokesperson.According to Der Spiegel, Ballout told the Berlin court this spring that he had distanced himself from extremist ideology and violence.Thomas Mücke, an extremism expert at the Violence Prevention Network VPN, told ARD television that he had met the suspect.He said Ballout had given social workers "a very composed, very cautious, very controlled and very friendly impression"."And those are precisely the criteria where we realise we can't really get to know the person," he continued.Some have called for Germany's laws against terrorism to be made stricter.Peter Neumann at King's College London told ZDF that Germany's criminal law on terrorism is "too lenient," and sentences too short by European standards.He also called for a rethink of Germany's juvenile justice system, which he said prioritises education rather than the protection of the public.The home affairs spokesperson for the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), Sebastian Fiedler, told Deutschlandfunk radio that criminal law was not the problem, but the way it was applied."We need to look more closely at why [Ballout] still at large. Another key question is: 'What actually happened after his release from prison? Who was he still in contact with?' Although he was under surveillance, there was clearly a gap in the system."Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was too early to say what political consequences will be drawn from the attack, but promised there would be action: "We will have to respond with prudence, but also with determination."He said if individuals classified as threats could not be detained, their freedom of movement should be restricted "as much as possible.""I cannot understand how I can track my mobile phone from anywhere in the world... yet it is supposedly impossible, or technically unfeasible, for security authorities in Germany to determine the whereabouts of individuals classified as security threats to that same extent."He said he had asked the interior ministry to review the law regarding monitoring jurisdiction.

schema.headline: Anger as Berlin Pride attacker revealed to have been freed weeks earlier

title: On the front line of Ecuador's drugs war, police fight drug gangs
description: Image source, Lee Durant/BBCByOrla GuerinSenior international correspondent, in EcuadorIn the Ecuadoran city of Durán, riddled with drugs and rival ga
body: Image source, Lee Durant/BBCByOrla GuerinSenior international correspondent, in EcuadorIn the Ecuadoran city of Durán, riddled with drugs and rival gangs, Police Captain Jean Carlos Bustamante knows exactly what he is up against – not just the criminals who kill and sometimes dismember their rivals, but also the enemy within."We have many, many bad people inside our unit, inside the state, inside politics," he says. "We have many, many guys that are corrupt. They are in the pay of the gangs."The only police officers he can trust, he says, are the ones right beside him - members of his hand-picked team. At 34, Captain Bustamante is the oldest among them and moves like the special forces officer he used to be.With the sun setting, he leads his team into a hardscrabble neighbourhood where windows are sealed off behind metal grills, and lips are sealed by fear.  This is the heart of gangland, controlled by a group called Los Aguilas (Spanish for The Eagles).I ask what happens if local people speak out against the gangs. "They kill them," the captain replies. "So that's why they never say nothing."Figure caption, Confronting gang members at the heart of Ecuador's drug battleHe's heading for an abandoned house where he believes weapons have been hidden (gunmen don't keep their guns at home). He and his team line up, hugging the wall, heavily armed, and tightly packed. A battering ram gets them through the door.They find two handguns – one rusty but the other ready to be fired - and ammunition for an assault rifle.The captain says he's happy with the result. "The first reason is because we are safe," he says. "The second is that there are two guns less for the gangs."But this is a small victory, in a war of attrition. He admits the gangs have "many weapons and much more money than the state".He knows the risks only too well – having lost three close friends fighting the gangs. He has also lost his fear he says, "years ago", but his parents have not."My mum says 'be careful, maybe you can die there'," he tells me. "My dad calls all the time and asks 'my son, are you good? Tell me that you are good.'"A line can be traced - in dollars and in broken lives - from the back streets of Durán to the hotspots of London, and other capital cities. Around 70% of the cocaine reaching Europe and the US is funnelled out of Ecuador, according to the country's President, Daniel Noboa.How did it come to this?The drug pours in from neighbouring Colombia and Peru – the two biggest producers in the world. Powerful home-grown gangs – with links to Mexican cartels and Albanian mafia groups – help smuggle the cocaine onwards. They take advantage of Ecuador's weak border controls, underfunded security forces, and long Pacific coast.In the process what was a peaceful tourist haven in South America has – in under a decade - become a killing ground.Last year the murder rate was one of the highest in the world, with more than 9,200 people killed, according to Ecuador's interior ministry. That's despite an iron-fisted crackdown by President Noboa over the past two years. Critics say it has backfired. Top crime bosses have been arrested, causing the gangs to fracture, but also to multiply.Many here believe the war against the gangs will never be won.Captain Bustamante keeps fighting.When we join him for another operation he's lying in wait getting a bird's eye view of the back alleys from a drone. He sees three figures moving around at the edge of a playground – "micro-traffickers" - caught in the act, he says. They are at the bottom of the drug chain, selling locally, in minute amounts, not kilos.Within minutes he and his team have tracked the suspects to their door. The battering ram is out again, and soon they are in the kitchen, where a middle-aged woman protests, and a young girl bursts into tears.The police move from room to room, by torchlight - there's no power - opening wardrobes and lifting mattresses. Upstairs, they find a hiding place behind a window. A young suspect emerges and is detained. Two others are handcuffed in another room. All three are led away, denying that there were dealing drugs.Nearby the captain finds tiny paper packets of "H" stashed in a flowerpot. It's a highly addictive mix containing small amounts of heroin sold by neighbourhood dealers for $1.00 (£0.75) per packet.One of the suspects is charged, and if convicted, he could get five years in jail. Prosecutors release the other two. Senior officers say that happens a lot. They blame corruption in the justice system, and the prosecutor's office.Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Even when police capture criminals and drugs, they complain corruption in the justice system prevents real change"We imprison them [gang members] and they release them," says Colonel Santiago Gavilanez, deputy commander of Durán police. "We know because when we carry out raids, we recapture them. Some of those who are released kill people and leave orphans behind." He tells us that the gangs have money to "buy laws, judges, and politicians".We get an example of the buying power of the gangs from another police officer, in a different location. For his safety, we cannot reveal his name or where he is based.  He told us he was contacted twice by text and offered a massive bribe - "enough money to retire on". He turned it down. Someone – a colleague perhaps – had informed the gang exactly where he worked and what he did. "You never know who is watching," he said. We heard that a lot during a week in Durán, and surrounding areas.Back at the playground it's the end of another long day in body armour, but Captain Bustamante says he has to keep going.  "Maybe, I am a little tired," he admits, "but it's my work. I believe we can win this war. We have to do it."As we speak, one of the main gang bosses in the area has been spotted nearby. "We know he controls the dealers," says the captain, "but we have no leads or evidence, so we can't arrest him".But police here insist they are having an impact. The murder rate in Durán is down by half, they say, in the first six months of this year.Image caption, Guayas, the province where Durán is located, had the highest number of violent deaths last yearThere are other indications of progress, they tell us, with streets no longer deserted after 19:00 local time, and bodies no longer found beheaded or dismembered. That used to be common, according to Colonel Gavilanez. "We have managed to contain the gangs," he says. "Getting complete control is going to be a medium-term process."Elsewhere the criminals are containing the police. Through a contact we arranged to meet a local gang on their home turf, about an hour's drive from the city. Their leader – whom we are calling Jonathan – told me he had four officers on his payroll."Whenever they're going to do an operation, they call me," he said. "They tell me to hide things, and to get out of here. When they arrive, they find nothing."That early warning systems costs him about $1,500 (£1,100) to $2,000 (£1,500) a month.Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Jonathan - not his real name - says he has four police officers on his payrollAt 37, Jonathan is just a few years older than Captain Bustamante, but he's across enemy lines. He says he joined a gang, at 18, to put food on the table.He and his men (and boys) strolled through the rough-hewn streets, in broad daylight, brandishing weapons - including a semi-automatic rifle and a pistol. The youngest gang member we saw was a lean 17-year-old, wearing a bulletproof vest, and flip flops.  All covered their faces.Jonathan answered our questions inside a narrow room in a breeze block house, with his lieutenants crowding in. Most of the space was taken up by a bed. He admitted to being a drug pusher and a killer. "How many lives have you taken?" I asked."Well, until now about eight, I think. I don't remember well," he replied, with a handgun in his lap, pointing in my direction.Jonathan claimed his gang didn't kill innocent people, just a rival criminal group trying to replace them. "They want to force their way in here," he said, "they come killing people, and we respond. The main thing for us now is to eliminate the other gang."As we spoke, local people gathered near the doorway, children among them. Human rights workers in Ecuador told us boys can be recruited into gang life by the age of 12. Three years later they can be hitmen.Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Gang members walk openly down the streets in broad daylight with weaponsJonathan makes no apologies for putting guns in the hands of teenagers or selling cocaine in the neighbourhood he claims to protect. He insists the drug trade cannot be rooted out."I think it's an issue that will never end," he says. "If they shut us down, another one [gang] will come along, and if they shut that one down, there will be another."He expects to die, as he has lived – by the gun. "Death is paid by death," he said. "But if they come to kill me, I won't make it easy for them."Two nights later, back in Durán, we saw how gangs settle scores. The body of a man was visible under flashing police lights, lying where he fell, beside a motorbike. Bullet casings were still on the ground. Neighbours stood looking on, mostly in silence.A man and woman held each other and wept – relatives of the dead man.Police suspected a revenge attack – one gang against another.Forensic teams lifted the body onto a stretcher, and into the back of a refrigerated van: violent death, on repeat. Another corpse was already inside.Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption, Violent deaths have skyrocketed in Ecuador over the last 10 yearsA witness was willing to speak – but not to be named.  "He already had a bullet in his back," he told us. "As he fell, they finished him off with a shot to the head. He was shot six times by two men on a motorbike.""We are used to this now because it happens every day," he said. "You might just step outside and catch a stray bullet. You can't even go out or talk to friends or family because someone could shoot you."He does not expect the president's fight against the gangs to deliver any change."Criminals are like ghosts," he said, in a low voice. "They pop up wherever they please."Then he melted away, into the warm night air.You never know who is watching.With additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Chris GibsonEcuadorDrugs trade

schema.headline: On the front line of Ecuador's drugs war, police fight drug gangs
